title: Borrowed $100 from his mother to launch his first ferry boat
statement: At sixteen, borrowed one hundred dollars from his mother to buy the periauger Swiftsure and launched his own freight-and-passenger ferry between Staten Island and Manhattan, having quit school at eleven to work his father's boat.
outcome: The ferry operation grew into a fleet of small boats and a working mastery of ship design, positioning him to take command of Thomas Gibbons's steamboat in 1817 and build a regional shipping empire.

title: Founded the Accessory Transit Company across Nicaragua
statement: Pivoted from regional steamboat lines to ocean steamships at the start of the California gold rush, founding the Accessory Transit Company to carry passengers across Nicaragua by lake, river, and a twelve-mile carriage road after failing to raise capital for a canal.
outcome: The line became the cheapest route to California, carrying about 2,000 passengers a month; after the Walker filibuster wrecked the route, Vanderbilt converted the wreckage into a $40,000 monthly stipend from Pacific Mail and US Mail, later raised to $56,000.

title: Pivoted from steamships to railroads by taking the New York and Harlem
statement: Took control of the New York and Harlem Railroad in a famous stock-market corner at sixty-nine and was elected president, later explaining he wanted to prove he could take a worthless railroad and make it valuable; he sold his last ships in 1864.
outcome: He added the Hudson River Railroad in 1864, the New York Central in 1867, and the Lake Shore and Michigan Southern in 1869, merging his key lines under the New York Central and Hudson River Railroad, among the biggest corporations the United States had yet seen.

title: Cornered Harlem stock a second time to ruin the short-selling legislators
statement: After an Albany Senate committee killed the Harlem's Broadway franchise bill, with Daniel Drew and New York Central officials secretly shorting the stock, Vanderbilt resolved to run the corner again, assembling roughly $5 million with Tobin and Leonard Jerome to buy the equivalent of the entire capital stock plus 27,000 shares.
outcome: The last short contracts settled at 285 in late June 1864 with losses above a million dollars and bankruptcies among the shorts; Vanderbilt exulted that they had busted the whole legislature, netting about $2 million and total control of the road.

title: Blockaded Albany and seized control of the New York Central
statement: On January 14, 1867, cut the Hudson River Railroad's through ticketing and baggage arrangements with the New York Central, terminating all traffic at East Albany and briefly severing New York City's rail connection to the West, after the Central rebuffed his lease offers.
outcome: Stockholders led by Edward Cunard and John Jacob Astor Jr., representing over $13 million of stock, invited him to take their proxies; at the December 1867 election his $18 million ballot decided control and he was elected president of the New York Central.

title: Waged the Erie War against Drew, Gould, and Fisk
statement: Attempted to corner the stock of the Erie Railway to punish treasurer Daniel Drew, who conspired with Jay Gould and James Fisk to flood Wall Street with watered shares issued in defiance of state law restricting share issuance.
outcome: Vanderbilt lost more than $7 million before a compromise, secured through the leverage of a corrupt judge's arrest warrants and the threat of litigation, returned most of the money; the trio kept the Erie while Vanderbilt remained the richest man in America.

title: Built Grand Central Depot as his railroads' New York terminus
statement: Directed the New York and Harlem in 1869 to begin construction of Grand Central Depot on 42nd Street, uniting the Harlem, Hudson River, and New Haven lines at a single station and sinking the Fourth Avenue tracks in a cut that later became a tunnel.
outcome: The Second Empire depot, completed in October 1871, was considered the country's first station to measure up to those of Europe; Fourth Avenue became Park Avenue, and the site was rebuilt as Grand Central Terminal in 1913.

title: Endowed Vanderbilt University with a $1 million gift
statement: Gave Bishop Holland McTyeire one million dollars to found Vanderbilt University in Nashville, at that date the largest single act of philanthropy in American history, intending to strengthen the ties between the sections of the country after the Civil War.
outcome: The university enrolled its first students in the fall of 1875 backed by a $600,000 working endowment after William's additional $200,000 gift, and in 1914 the Tennessee Supreme Court ruled that the Commodore, not the Methodist Church, was its founder.
